title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8 Secundo close: Ep. 107, Prosper, Fulgentius—vivifying grace not seized by native liberty
pass_a_gloss: The last testimony we bring from Augustine will be that which stands in Epistle 107, where against the Pelagians he reviews twelve sentences belonging to the catholic faith, of which the fourth is, We know that the grace of God is not given to all human beings. But lest anyone pretend that by the death of Christ this has been effected, that this grace is prepared and offered to all, although it is had or not had according as human beings have willed to receive it or not to receive it, this also is excluded by the fifth and sixth sentence: concerning which matter we will say more presently. From Augustine let us descend to Prosper. To the Genoese Excerpts, Response to doubt 7, he says that when the word of truth is preached, some believe by will, others do not believe; but when God has opened the hearts of those, but has not opened the hearts of those. Which is just as if he had said that the grace of faith is given to certain ones, denied to others. And Response to the eighth doubt: Concerning the Tyrians and Sidonians what else can we say than that it was not given them that they should believe? But why this was denied them, let them say if they can, etc. Prosper asserts two things: one, That the gift of faith is denied to certain human beings; the other, That the cause why it is denied is inscrutable. Finally, in the book On the Ungrateful, chapter 6, he sets out as the Pelagians' error, That without choice either the law or the grace of Christ wills to save every human being; and that the gift of the Caller is so set forth that no one cannot come to it by his own liberty and proper strength. Then he paints the Semi-Pelagians' opinion in these colors in chapter 10; which in chapter 11 he rejects with these words: Say, whence you prove that the grace of Christ passes by absolutely no human being of all who are born? Therefore with Prosper it is counted a fiber of Pelagian poison if anyone defends grace given to all. Let us now hear Fulgentius. He in the book On the Truth of Predestination has these things: The holy Fathers, holding the truth of apostolic preaching, most certainly knew, and left in books to be known, that the grace of God is not given generally to all human beings. A little after: No human being will be able to desire or ask that grace itself, nor even to know it, unless he first receive it from God. The same in the same place: Let us not therefore think that the grace of God is given to all human beings. For not of all is faith, and certain ones do not receive the charity of God that they may be saved: In whom nevertheless, that they do not believe nor love the Lord, it is the fault of the human will, which, so long as it is not changed by the grace of the divine gift, either does not understand God's precepts, or despises them understood, etc. What plainer, if Fulgentius be heard, than that vivifying grace is not given to all by God, nor can be had by any to whom it has not been given from above? If clearer things are desired, I add that from the book On the Incarnation and Grace of Jesus Christ, page 89: God who prepares the will himself gives it. Which will, if God has not given to the human being by his grace, the human being can never will to believe in God, because grace does not find the will, but works it in the human being. You see that the sentence of those Fathers who declared war on Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians is concordant: Vivifying and saving grace is not given to all human beings; and the vitiated will to which it is not given can indeed by its own fault disdain grace and repel it offered in external means; but cannot snatch this vivifying grace by right of its inborn liberty and drag it to itself.
pass_b_english: Our last Augustine witness is Epistle 107. Against the Pelagians he lists twelve catholic sentences; the fourth is, We know God's grace is not given to all. And lest anyone claim Christ's death made this grace prepared and offered to everyone, had or missed only as people choose to take or refuse it, sentences five and six shut that door too—more on that shortly. From Augustine we come to Prosper. In the Genoese Excerpts, answer to doubt 7: when the word of truth is preached, some believe willingly and some do not—but only because God has opened some hearts and not others. That is to say, the grace of faith is given to some and denied to others. Answer to the eighth doubt: of Tyre and Sidon what can we say but that it was not given them to believe? Why denied—let them tell if they can. Prosper asserts two things: the gift of faith is denied to some, and the reason is unsearchable. In On the Ungrateful 6 he sets out the Pelagian error: that without choosing persons, law or Christ's grace wills to save every human, and the Caller's gift is so laid open that anyone can reach it by his own liberty and strength. Chapter 10 paints the Semi-Pelagian colors; chapter 11 rejects them: Tell us how you prove Christ's grace passes by none of all who are born. For Prosper, to defend grace given to all is a strand of Pelagian poison. Hear Fulgentius. On the Truth of Predestination: the holy Fathers, holding apostolic truth, knew for certain—and left it in books—that God's grace is not given generally to all. A little later: no one can desire, ask, or even know that grace unless he first receives it from God. Again: do not think God's grace is given to all. Not all have faith; some do not receive God's charity so as to be saved. That they neither believe nor love the Lord is the fault of the human will, which, until divine gift-grace changes it, either fails to understand God's commands or despises them once understood. What could be plainer? Vivifying grace is not given to all, and no one has it unless it is given from above. Clearer still, On the Incarnation and Grace of Jesus Christ, p. 89: God who prepares the will is the One who gives it. If he has not given that will by his grace, a person can never will to believe in God—because grace does not find the will ready; it works the will in the person. So the Fathers who warred on Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians speak with one voice: vivifying, saving grace is not given to all; the spoiled will that lacks it can by its own fault scorn grace and push away what is offered in outward means; but it cannot, by right of native liberty, snatch this life-giving grace and drag it to itself.
source_text: Ultimum testimonium quod ex Augustino afferimus, erit illud quod exstat Epistola 107, ubi recenset contra Pelagianos duodecim sententias ad fidem catholicam pertinentes, quarum quarta est, Scimus gratiam Dei non dari omnibus hominibus. Ne autem quis obtendat, morte Christi id effectum esse ut omnibus praeparetur et offeratur haec gratia, quamvis habeatur aut non habeatur prout homines eam accipere aut non accipere voluerint, hoc etiam sententia quinta et sexta excluditur: Qua de re plura mox dicemus. Ab Augustino ad Prosperum descendamus. Ad Excerpta Genuens. Resp. ad dub. 7. dicit, Cum verbum veritatis praedicatur, alios voluntate credere, alios non credere; sed cum illorum corda Deus aperuerit, illorum autem non aperuerit. Quod perinde est ac si dixisset, gratiam fidei dari quibusdam, negari aliis. Et Resp. ad dub. octavum, De Tyriis et Sidoniis quid aliud possumus dicere quam, non esse eis datum ut crederent? Quare autem hoc eis negatum fuerit, dicant si possunt, &c. Duo asserit Prosper: unum, Quod donum fidei negetur quibusdam hominibus; alterum, Quod causa cur negetur sit inscrutabilis. Denique, in libro De Ingratis, cap. 6. tanquam Pelagianorum errorem proponit, Quod sine dilectu seu lex seu gratia Christi omnem hominem salvare velit; donumque vocantis sic sit propositum ut nullus non possit ad illud libertate sua proprioque vigore venire. Dein Semipelagianorum sententiam depingit, hisce coloribus, Cap. 10; quam capite 11. rejicit hisce verbis: Dic, unde probes quod gratia Christi nullum omnino hominem de cunctis qui generantur praetereat? Prospero igitur habetur Pelagianae virulentiae fibra, si quis gratiam omnibus datam defendat. Fulgentium jam audiamus. Is in libro De verit. praedest. haec habet: Sancti Patres, Apostolicae praedicationis tenentes veritatem, certissime cognoverunt, cognoscendaque libris reliquerunt, gratiam Dei non omnibus hominibus generaliter dari. Paulo post: Ipsam gratiam nullus hominum desiderare vel poscere, sed nec cognoscere poterit, nisi eam prius a Deo accipiat. Idem ibidem: Non ergo putemus gratiam Dei omnibus hominibus dari. Non enim omnium est fides, et quidam charitatem Dei non recipiunt ut salvi fiant: In quibus tamen, ut non credant, neque diligant Dominum, humanae voluntatis est vitium, quae, quandiu gratia Divini muneris non mutatur, aut praecepta Dei non intelligit, aut intellecta contemnit, &c. Quid apertius, quam, si Fulgentius audiatur, gratiam vivificantem non dari omnibus a Deo, nec posse ab ullo haberi cui non desuper data fuerit? Si clariora desiderentur, addo illud ex libro De incarnat. et grat. Jesu Christi, pag. 89: Deus qui voluntatem praeparat, ipse eam donat. Quam si Deus per suam gratiam homini non dederit, nunquam potest homo in Deum velle credere, quia ipsam voluntatem gratia non invenit, sed operatur in homine. Videtis esse concordem eorum Patrum sententiam, qui Pelagianis et Semipelagianis bellum indixerunt: Gratiam vivificantem et salutiferam non dari omnibus hominibus; ac voluntatem vitiatam cui non datur, posse quidem suo vitio gratiam fastidire, et in mediis externis oblatam repellere; non posse autem hanc vivificam gratiam pro jure innatae suae libertatis arripere, et ad se pertrahere.
